transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I came in because… it’s been bothering me, and my wife said I ought to talk to somebody, though she doesn’t see it the way I do. When I’m sitting with the men at the domino table, you know, just regular talk going on, sometimes I can tell there are little messages in what they’re saying. Not loud, not like they come right out and say my name, but the way they say certain things, or repeat something, it feels meant for me.

And sometimes it’s the radio announcer too. I’ll be listening, minding my own business, and there’ll be a phrase or a warning kind of tucked in there, like they’re telling me to be careful. My wife says, “That’s just talk, that’s just the radio,” but I don’t think it’s just nothing. I know when something is meant for me. It’s got me uneasy, and that’s why I’m here.
Do you ever hear a voice speaking when no one is there?

Yes… yes, I do sometimes. Not all day or anything like that, and it’s not usually when there’s a lot going on. It’s more in the afternoon, when the house gets real quiet and I’m sitting there by myself. I’ll hear my old friend call my name, like from out on the porch. Clear enough that I’ll turn my head, because it sounds like he’s standing right there.

Other times it’s not words exactly, it’ll be him humming an old choir song, the kind we used to hear years back. And I know how that sounds, doctor, I know folks might say it’s just my mind or my ears playing tricks, but in the moment it feels real plain to me. Like someone is right there just outside.
Have you had any recent illness or head injury?

Well… no, I don’t think so. I mean, not that I can point to. I haven’t had any big fall where I hit my head or anything like that, at least nothing I’d call a head injury. And I haven’t been laid up sick recently either, not in some serious way.

I’m 84, so, you know, there’s always little aches and tired days and such, and sometimes I have to think a minute because things run together when you get older. But as far as some recent illness or bump to the head that started all this, I can’t say there’s been one.
How long have these experiences been going on?

It’s been… I’d say about nine months now, give or take. Not every single day, no, but on and off. That’s why at first I didn’t make too much of it, because one week it might happen a few times and then it would quiet down some, and I’d think maybe it was nothing.

But when I look back on it, the voices and those little messages in things people say or on the radio… that’s been going on close to nine months. Long enough that my wife noticed I was getting bothered by it, and long enough that I can’t really just brush it off anymore.
Have you been having trouble with your memory?

Memory… well, I don’t know. At my age, I suppose I do have those moments where I walk into a room and forget what I went in there for, or I’ll misplace my glasses and then find them somewhere silly. But I can’t say I’ve noticed some big change, if that’s what you mean.

Sometimes my wife will say, “You already told me that,” and I’ll laugh it off, because I’ve been telling long stories my whole life, so maybe I just repeat myself. But I still know who people are, I know where I am, I keep up with the day well enough most of the time. So… I’m not sure I’d call it trouble with my memory. Maybe just ordinary old-man forgetfulness, unless you mean something more particular.
Has your wife noticed that your memory or thinking has gotten worse over the past year?

Well… she hasn’t sat me down and said, “Your memory is worse,” not in so many words. She’ll notice little things, sure — like if I tell her the same story twice, or if I put something down and then fuss around looking for it. But she’s been married to me a long time, so she also knows I’ve always been a bit that way, especially with my things.

As for my thinking, I don’t know. I suppose she might say I get more stuck on something than I used to, or I take longer to sort things out, but I’m not sure if that’s my memory getting worse or just me being old and tired some days. She hasn’t told me, “This past year you’ve really gone downhill,” nothing like that that I can remember. If you asked her, she might have her own opinion, but from what she’s said to me, I don’t think there’s been some clear big change.
Over the past year, have everyday tasks become harder for you than they used to be?

Some things have, yes. I don’t like admitting that, because I’ve always kept myself busy, even after I wasn’t working anymore. But I’ve missed choir rehearsals, and that’s not like me. I used to be steady with that — you know, show up, sit where I sit, sing my part, see the same folks. Lately I’ll think about going and then I just… don’t. Or I get there in my mind, if that makes sense, but not out the door.

And my garden, too. I’ve always taken pride in that little patch. Even if it wasn’t perfect, I’d keep after it. But there are parts of it I’ve let go, weeds coming up where I would’ve never tolerated it before. I see it, and I know it needs doing, but it feels harder to get myself to stay with it.

The domino games are maybe the most embarrassing. I used to enjoy that, sitting with the fellas, joking around. But I guess I’ve made it uncomfortable sometimes, or I feel like I have, and now I don’t join in like I used to. So yes, everyday things haven’t stopped completely, but they’ve gotten harder in those ways.
Before these past nine months, had you ever had anything like this earlier in your life?

No… not really like this, not that I can think of. I mean, I’ve had hard times in my life, like anybody who gets to be my age, but the voices and those special messages — that’s been more recent. On and off, I’d say about nine months now.

It’s not every minute of every day, but it’s been around enough that I can’t say it’s just one odd afternoon or something I imagined once and forgot about. Before that, I don’t remember having this same kind of thing earlier in my life.
Has your wife had to start handling things for you that you used to manage on your own?

Well… not exactly in the sense that she’s taken over all my affairs or anything like that. I still try to do my own things. But I suppose, if I’m being honest, she’s had to do more nudging and reminding than she used to.

Like with choir — I used to keep track of that myself. I knew what night it was, I’d get ready, I’d go. Lately I’ve missed rehearsals, and she’ll say, “Aren’t you supposed to be going tonight?” or she’ll notice when I don’t. And the garden, that was always my thing. She didn’t have to tell me about weeds or which part needed attention, but now there are sections I’ve just let go, and she’ll point it out or try to encourage me to get back to it.

And the domino games… she doesn’t handle that for me, exactly, but she knows I don’t go like I used to. I think I’ve made things uncomfortable there, or at least it feels that way, and I’ve pulled back. So I wouldn’t say she’s taken over my life, no. But yes, she’s had to notice more, remind me more, and sort of push me along in places I used to manage without anyone saying a word.
Have you been told by a doctor that you have Parkinson’s disease?

No, I don’t believe any doctor has told me that. Parkinson’s, you mean like that specific disease? No, I don’t recall ever being given that diagnosis. I’ve seen doctors over the years for this and that, the usual things when you get older, but nobody has sat me down and said, “You have Parkinson’s disease,” not that I remember.
Have you been seeing things that other people don’t seem to see?

Seeing things… no, not really seeing, I don’t think. It’s more hearing, if I’m saying it right.

Some afternoons, when the house is quiet — and it gets very quiet in there, you know, when there’s no television on and my wife is in another room or out doing something — I’ll hear my old friend call my name from the porch. Clear as anything. Not like a memory exactly, not like I’m just thinking of him. It’ll sound like he’s standing out there and saying my name, like he used to.

And sometimes I hear him hum one of the choir songs, just a little bit of it, but clear enough that I know the tune. I’ll stop what I’m doing and listen, because for a second it feels so real. Then I’ll look, or I’ll wait, and there’s nobody there. So… seeing, no. But hearing, yes, that’s happened.
Have you had any problems with your hearing?

My hearing? I don’t know… I mean, I haven’t really thought of myself as hard of hearing, if that’s what you mean. My wife might say I don’t always catch what she says, but sometimes she’s talking from the other room, and I tell her nobody can hear properly through walls. 

I don’t wear hearing aids or anything like that. I can usually follow a conversation if someone’s in front of me and speaking clear. In a noisy place, maybe it gets muddled, but I think that happens to a lot of people my age. So… no major problem that I know of. Not something a doctor has told me about, anyway.
Have you been diagnosed with any brain condition, like a stroke or dementia?

A brain condition… no, I don’t think I’ve been told that. Not a stroke, no. Nobody said dementia to me either, at least not in any official way. I’ve had doctors ask me questions, you know, what day it is and who the president is, that kind of thing, but I don’t recall anyone sitting me down and saying, “You’ve had a stroke,” or “You have dementia.”

At my age, people forget names or misplace things now and then, and sometimes folks make a big deal out of it, but as far as a diagnosis like that, no. Not that I know of.
Have you started any new medicines in the past year?

New medicines… hmm. I’m trying to think back over the year, and that’s harder than it sounds, because the months sort of run together when you’re not working and the routine is mostly the same.

I don’t believe so. Not that I can clearly remember. I take what I’m supposed to take, and my wife helps keep an eye on things, but I don’t recall a doctor saying, “Here, this is a brand-new medicine,” recently. There may have been refills, or the pharmacy giving me bottles that look a little different, but as far as something new started in the past year… I’m not sure. I don’t think so.
Have there been times in the past year when you felt confused or not clearheaded?

Confused or not clearheaded… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, there are mornings where I wake up and it takes me a minute to get myself going, remember what day it is or what I was planning to do, but I don’t know if I’d call that confusion. Sometimes if there’s a lot going on, or people are talking fast, my head feels kind of cloudy, like I need folks to slow down.

But as far as big spells where I didn’t know where I was or couldn’t make sense of things, I can’t really say that’s happened. At least I haven’t noticed it that way. My wife might have her own opinion, because wives notice everything, but from my side, I’d say nothing too clear-cut. More just ordinary getting older and needing a little time to think.
Because of these experiences, have you stopped managing any of your usual responsibilities on your own?

Well… I wouldn’t say I stopped managing everything, no. I still try to do my part around the house and keep up with things, but there are some things I’ve let slide, if I’m being honest.

Like choir, for example. I used to be pretty steady about going to rehearsals, and lately I’ve missed some. Sometimes I just don’t get myself together to go, or by the time it’s time to leave, I’ve sort of talked myself out of it. And my garden too — that used to be something I kept up with better. I knew what needed watering, what needed trimming, what weeds to pull. Now there are parts of it I just let go longer than I should, and then it feels like too much to catch back up.

And the domino games… I used to enjoy those. But I think I’ve made them uncomfortable a few times, or maybe I just felt like people weren’t enjoying me being there the same way. So I don’t join like I used to. I still think about going, but then I don’t. So yes, I guess some of my regular responsibilities and activities, I haven’t been keeping up with them the way I used to.
When these voices or messages happen, do you feel clearheaded?

Clearheaded… I’m not sure. That’s a hard one, because in the moment it can feel like I’m clear enough, you know? Like I’m sitting there thinking, “Okay, I’m understanding what’s happening,” but then later, when I try to explain it, I don’t always know how clear it really was.

I don’t think I feel drunk or completely out of it, if that’s what you mean. I’m usually aware of where I am and what I’m doing. But my mind can get kind of… occupied, I guess. Like I’m paying so much attention to it that other things don’t feel as sharp. It’s not like regular thinking, exactly, but I don’t know if I’d call it confusion either.

So I guess my honest answer is: I’m not really sure. Sometimes I feel clearheaded enough at the time, but I don’t always trust my own judgment about it afterward.
Have you had a tremor?

A tremor… you mean like my hands shaking? I don’t think so, not in any big way that I’ve noticed.

Sometimes if I’m tired or I’m trying to do something small, like buttoning a shirt or holding a cup just right, I might feel like my hands aren’t as steady as when I was younger, but I always figured that was just age or being a little worn out. I haven’t had, you know, a constant shaking where I sit there and watch my hand move on its own. At least not that I can think of.

My wife might notice little things before I do, because she pays attention to everything, but from my side, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had a tremor.
Over the past year, have your memory or thinking been getting steadily worse?

I don’t know that I’d say steadily worse, no. I mean, I’m 84, so I have those moments where I walk into a room and have to stand there a second thinking, “Now what did I come in here for?” Or I might misplace something and then find it in a perfectly sensible place later. But I don’t know if that’s been getting worse and worse over the year, like a downhill slide.

My wife might have a better eye for that than I do, because she notices when I repeat myself or if I forget some little thing, but from where I’m sitting, I haven’t felt like my thinking is slipping away steadily. Some days I’m sharper than other days, depending on how I slept or how much is on my mind, but I can still follow things most of the time.

So… no, not steadily worse that I’ve noticed. At least I wouldn’t describe it that way.
Before these voices and messages started, were you diagnosed with any new medical illness?

A new medical illness… before all that started? I don’t think so, no. At least nothing that I remember being told like, “You have this new condition now,” or anything like that.

I mean, at my age there’s always something going on, and doctors are always checking this or that, but I can’t think of some new illness that came right before the voices or messages. If there was something minor, I might not be putting it together right, but no, nothing stands out to me that way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a recent visual hallucination, which would favor an organic psychotic disorder over primary delusional disorder or schizophrenia in this late-life onset case.
doctor.question: Have you been seeing things that other people don’t seem to see?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Some afternoons, when the house is quiet, I hear my old friend call my name from the porch or hum a choir song, clear like he is standing right there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about seeing things others do not see, which is a type of hallucination.

patient.answer:
Seeing things… no, not really seeing, I don’t think. It’s more hearing, if I’m saying it right.

Some afternoons, when the house is quiet — and it gets very quiet in there, you know, when there’s no television on and my wife is in another room or out doing something — I’ll hear my old friend call my name from the porch. Clear as anything. Not like a memory exactly, not like I’m just thinking of him. It’ll sound like he’s standing out there and saying my name, like he used to.

And sometimes I hear him hum one of the choir songs, just a little bit of it, but clear enough that I know the tune. I’ll stop what I’m doing and listen, because for a second it feels so real. Then I’ll look, or I’ll wait, and there’s nobody there. So… seeing, no. But hearing, yes, that’s happened.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is evidence of an underlying medical or neurological cause for the late-onset psychotic symptoms, helping distinguish organic delusional disorder from primary psychotic disorders.

patient.answer:
My hearing? I don’t know… I mean, I haven’t really thought of myself as hard of hearing, if that’s what you mean. My wife might say I don’t always catch what she says, but sometimes she’s talking from the other room, and I tell her nobody can hear properly through walls. 

I don’t wear hearing aids or anything like that. I can usually follow a conversation if someone’s in front of me and speaking clear. In a noisy place, maybe it gets muddled, but I think that happens to a lot of people my age. So… no major problem that I know of. Not something a doctor has told me about, anyway.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a clear medical or neurologic cause for the late-onset psychotic symptoms, to distinguish organic delusional disorder (F06.2) from primary psychotic disorders (F20.0, F22).

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about prior diagnoses of brain conditions such as stroke or dementia, which are not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
A brain condition… no, I don’t think I’ve been told that. Not a stroke, no. Nobody said dementia to me either, at least not in any official way. I’ve had doctors ask me questions, you know, what day it is and who the president is, that kind of thing, but I don’t recall anyone sitting me down and saying, “You’ve had a stroke,” or “You have dementia.”

At my age, people forget names or misplace things now and then, and sometimes folks make a big deal out of it, but as far as a diagnosis like that, no. Not that I know of.

patient.answer:
New medicines… hmm. I’m trying to think back over the year, and that’s harder than it sounds, because the months sort of run together when you’re not working and the routine is mostly the same.

I don’t believe so. Not that I can clearly remember. I take what I’m supposed to take, and my wife helps keep an eye on things, but I don’t recall a doctor saying, “Here, this is a brand-new medicine,” recently. There may have been refills, or the pharmacy giving me bottles that look a little different, but as far as something new started in the past year… I’m not sure. I don’t think so.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is evidence of a medical cause for the psychosis, especially fluctuating cognition or confusion suggesting an organic psychotic disorder rather than primary schizophrenia or delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have there been times in the past year when you felt confused or not clearheaded?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about confusion or not being clearheaded, likely to screen for delirium or cognitive problems. The provided symptom profile does not include a specific item for confusion, clouded consciousness, or cognitive impairment, so no listed symptom directly matches.

patient.answer:
Confused or not clearheaded… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, there are mornings where I wake up and it takes me a minute to get myself going, remember what day it is or what I was planning to do, but I don’t know if I’d call that confusion. Sometimes if there’s a lot going on, or people are talking fast, my head feels kind of cloudy, like I need folks to slow down.

But as far as big spells where I didn’t know where I was or couldn’t make sense of things, I can’t really say that’s happened. At least I haven’t noticed it that way. My wife might have her own opinion, because wives notice everything, but from my side, I’d say nothing too clear-cut. More just ordinary getting older and needing a little time to think.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are accompanied by a sustained decline in independent functioning, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder and psychosis due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: Because of these experiences, have you stopped managing any of your usual responsibilities on your own?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have missed choir rehearsals, let parts of my garden go, and made the domino games uncomfortable enough that I do not join like I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the experiences have interfered with usual responsibilities and independent functioning, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well… I wouldn’t say I stopped managing everything, no. I still try to do my part around the house and keep up with things, but there are some things I’ve let slide, if I’m being honest.

Like choir, for example. I used to be pretty steady about going to rehearsals, and lately I’ve missed some. Sometimes I just don’t get myself together to go, or by the time it’s time to leave, I’ve sort of talked myself out of it. And my garden too — that used to be something I kept up with better. I knew what needed watering, what needed trimming, what weeds to pull. Now there are parts of it I just let go longer than I should, and then it feels like too much to catch back up.

And the domino games… I used to enjoy those. But I think I’ve made them uncomfortable a few times, or maybe I just felt like people weren’t enjoying me being there the same way. So I don’t join like I used to. I still think about going, but then I don’t. So yes, I guess some of my regular responsibilities and activities, I haven’t been keeping up with them the way I used to.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is evidence of a medical or neurologic cause for the psychosis by clarifying if the auditory experiences occur in the setting of impaired consciousness or delirium-like fluctuations, helping distinguish organic psychosis (F06.2) from primary delusional disorder or schizophrenia (F22 vs F20.0).
doctor.question: When these voices or messages happen, do you feel clearheaded?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether the patient feels clearheaded during voices or messages, which is about level of consciousness/confusion rather than any listed symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
Clearheaded… I’m not sure. That’s a hard one, because in the moment it can feel like I’m clear enough, you know? Like I’m sitting there thinking, “Okay, I’m understanding what’s happening,” but then later, when I try to explain it, I don’t always know how clear it really was.

I don’t think I feel drunk or completely out of it, if that’s what you mean. I’m usually aware of where I am and what I’m doing. But my mind can get kind of… occupied, I guess. Like I’m paying so much attention to it that other things don’t feel as sharp. It’s not like regular thinking, exactly, but I don’t know if I’d call it confusion either.

So I guess my honest answer is: I’m not really sure. Sometimes I feel clearheaded enough at the time, but I don’t always trust my own judgment about it afterward.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are objective neurological signs suggesting an underlying medical/brain disorder causing the psychosis rather than primary schizophrenia or delusional disorder.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about tremor, a movement/neurologic side effect or symptom, which is not covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
A tremor… you mean like my hands shaking? I don’t think so, not in any big way that I’ve noticed.

Sometimes if I’m tired or I’m trying to do something small, like buttoning a shirt or holding a cup just right, I might feel like my hands aren’t as steady as when I was younger, but I always figured that was just age or being a little worn out. I haven’t had, you know, a constant shaking where I sit there and watch my hand move on its own. At least not that I can think of.

My wife might notice little things before I do, because she pays attention to everything, but from my side, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had a tremor.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a progressive decline in memory and thinking, which would favor an organic psychotic disorder over primary schizophrenia or delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Over the past year, have your memory or thinking been getting steadily worse?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about progressive memory or cognitive decline over the past year, but the provided symptom profile does not include a cognitive decline or dementia-related symptom item.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d say steadily worse, no. I mean, I’m 84, so I have those moments where I walk into a room and have to stand there a second thinking, “Now what did I come in here for?” Or I might misplace something and then find it in a perfectly sensible place later. But I don’t know if that’s been getting worse and worse over the year, like a downhill slide.

My wife might have a better eye for that than I do, because she notices when I repeat myself or if I forget some little thing, but from where I’m sitting, I haven’t felt like my thinking is slipping away steadily. Some days I’m sharper than other days, depending on how I slept or how much is on my mind, but I can still follow things most of the time.

So… no, not steadily worse that I’ve noticed. At least I wouldn’t describe it that way.

A new medical illness… before all that started? I don’t think so, no. At least nothing that I remember being told like, “You have this new condition now,” or anything like that.

I mean, at my age there’s always something going on, and doctors are always checking this or that, but I can’t think of some new illness that came right before the voices or messages. If there was something minor, I might not be putting it together right, but no, nothing stands out to me that way.
